title: Repeating Decimals as Fractions
trouble: Students think 0.999… is a little less than 1.

blocks.html: In terminating and repeating decimals you saw that every fraction becomes a decimal that ends or repeats: $\frac{1}{4} = 0.25$ and $\frac{3}{11} = 0.272727\ldots = 0.\overline{27}$. Now go the other way, from a repeating decimal back to a fraction.

Let $x = 0.\overline{27}$. Multiplying by 100 moves every digit two places to the left: $100x = 27.\overline{27}$. Both numbers have exactly the same endless tail, so subtracting makes the tail disappear, and what is left is an ordinary equation.

head: value
blocks.cap: The tails line up, so they cancel.

blocks.html: To write a repeating decimal as a fraction, call it $x$. Multiply by 10, 100 or 1000 (one zero for each repeating digit) so the repeating parts line up, subtract, and solve for $x$.

blocks.title: Two repeating digits
blocks.q: Write $0.\overline{27}$ as a fraction in lowest terms.

blocks.title: The repeat starts later
steps: Only the 6 repeats. $10x = 1.\overline{6}$ and $100x = 16.\overline{6}$ have the same tail.

blocks.name: decimalgrid
blocks.cap: 0.99 leaves one hundredth uncovered, 0.999 would leave one thousandth, and so on. With 9s that never stop, no gap is left at all.

blocks.html: Thinking $0.\overline{9}$ is a little less than 1. Use the method: $x = 0.\overline{9}$, $10x = 9.\overline{9}$, so $9x = 9$ and $x = 1$. Another check: $\frac{1}{3} = 0.\overline{3}$, and three times each side gives $1 = 0.\overline{9}$. They are two names for one number; there is no number between them.
